extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of American political reform, political theory, and public policy
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and evaluative standards for what makes effective, legitimate, or dangerous political reformers and conceptions of democracy in the American context; covers qualities of reformers (Jerome, Hearst, Roosevelt) and normative conditions for democratic reconstruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify concrete remedial measures tied to public personality
rubrics_metrics.description: “A reformer must identify a particular group of remedial measures with his public personality. The public has a right to know in what definite ways a reformer's righteousness is to be made effective.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral superiority alone is insufficient for political leadership; reformers must specify definite policies and remedial measures that make their moral claims actionable. Candidates who rest on personal virtue without laying out concrete programs fail to lead public opinion effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take vigorous and novel lines on state and national politics
rubrics_metrics.description: Reformers should avoid reverting to old-fashioned, merely respectable or dull party doctrines and instead take vigorous, novel stances on state and national political problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text criticizes figures who lose vivacity when addressing public affairs and who default to conventional party thinking; successful reformers must show originality and energy rather than respectable dullness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply independent thought and 'intellectual veracity' to one's own party
rubrics_metrics.description: A genuine reformer must subject his own party's creed to critical scrutiny — applying his 'ideal of intellectual veracity' and 'instinct for consistency' to his party, not merely to opponents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of public evidence that a reformer has critically examined his party indicates intellectual complacency. Reform requires consistent, independent thought directed inward as well as outward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define 'liberal ideas' as progressive national ideas, not local heresies
rubrics_metrics.description: The adjective 'liberal' should denote progressive national ideas rather than local or radical political heresies (e.g., nullification, 'squatter' sovereignty, secession, free silver).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware conflating radical local dissatisfactions with liberalism; historical examples of so-called 'liberal ideas' are often expressions of localized discontent rather than genuine progressive national reform. Use a substantive, national standard when labeling parties or policies 'liberal.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid converting equal-rights rhetoric into revolutionary demagoguery
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of equal rights, in the hands of a fanatic or demagogue, can be converted into a revolutionary principle that legitimates vilification and punitive politics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns that rhetorical insistence on 'equal rights for all and special privileges for none' can be twisted into vindictive agitation against classes or individuals, undermining national integrity and democratic norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reform agitation must not rely on systematic vilification or factiousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic vilification of trusts, millionaires, or opponents (treating them as public enemies) is a characteristic of dangerous, factious reform agitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such methods (exposure, denunciation, holding up for public execration) resemble revolutionary tactics and exacerbate distrust and disgust, making wise and effective cures for social ills more difficult. Avoid sensationalist, exclusively punitive modes of agitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not remedy injustice by committing another injustice
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparing Hearstism to Abolitionist excesses: attempts to remedy one injustice by committing another (vilifying whole classes, inciting passions) harm the national fabric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reform methods must respect basic justice and national cohesion; violent or vindictive tactics that substitute one injustice for another are counterproductive and morally unacceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nationalize reform by linking it to the national idea and responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective reform should be identified with a national idea—making reform a matter of national organization and responsibility rather than merely local or negative agitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nationalization of reform endows the movement with dignity and constructive purpose. Reformers like Roosevelt are praised for connecting reform to a positive national program rather than only to denunciation or local grievances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use federal power constructively to regulate corporations in the public interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal government and the President can and should be used as instruments to regulate corporations and trusts when necessary for the national interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive national legislation and administrative action (e.g., regulating corporations) are legitimate tools of reform. This is presented as a positive Hamiltonian inheritance revitalized for modern democratic purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endorse responsible delegation and efficient national organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Delegation of authority and efficient national organization are not inherently undemocratic; they can be necessary to promote the national interest and strengthen democracy in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejects the Jeffersonian automatic distrust of delegated power. Practical reform may require empowering capable men and institutions with sufficient authority to serve the public good effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appoint competent officials and provide administrative machinery
rubrics_metrics.description: A reformer should appoint men of ability and supply them with administrative machinery that enables them to use their abilities for public advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical success in reform depends on administrative competence and institutions, not just rhetoric. Examples include civil service enforcement, police reform, taxation reforms, and regulatory administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for a democracy of individual and social improvement rather than mere individual rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Reform should move beyond a democracy defined solely by ambiguous claims of individual equal rights toward a democracy oriented to individual and social improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A democracy that only asserts equal individual rights risks being captured by factional or class interests; a national reform program should foster social progress and guard institutional integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage candid, consistent thinking and ensure ideas cohere with facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Reform movements need candid and consistent thought; ideas must square with the facts to which they are applied and with one another, and plain speaking must be justified by achievement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While practical action ('the hammer') may precede full intellectual development, long-term reform requires rigorous, coherent ideas. Reform leaders should cultivate both moral energy and intellectual discipline to avoid drifting into incoherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect individual liberties against the risk of popular despotism
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy defined as popular government risks sanctioning popular despotism; therefore the state must be organized so the sovereign power is deprived of legal opportunities to violate essential individual rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional and institutional safeguards (subordination of political liberties to civil liberties in practice) are necessary to secure individual freedom even within a framework of popular sovereignty. The Constitution is an instrument but popular sovereignty remains ultimate, so safeguards must be institutionalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure democracy's expressions of popular will do not destroy the continuity of sovereign power
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy must express the sovereign will in ways that do not contradict or destroy the continuous existence of its own sovereign power (avoid outcomes where popular will produces undemocratic or anti-institutional results).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (France: reactionary assemblies, plebiscitary delegations to dictators) show that popular majorities can produce undemocratic regimes. Democratic design must therefore prevent popular acts that undermine the democratic order itself.
